title: Opening at ang 1
tomorrow: what are the very first words on that first page?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one reading shared by a household, stumbles and all: read together. But every shared reading needs a first page.
screen: `READ TOGETHER.` → `EVERY READING NEEDS A FIRST PAGE.`

segments.voice: A brand-new notebook does something strange to people. Some skip the first page, scared to spoil it. Some tear it out after one bad line. A book as big as the Granth makes those nerves louder. So where does anyone start? The plain answer is the best one: where the Guru starts. Ang one.
screen: `THE FIRST PAGE OF A NEW NOTEBOOK.` → `WHERE DOES ANYONE START?` → `WHERE THE GURU STARTS: ANG ONE.`

segments.voice: Ang is the word Sikhs use for a page of the Granth. It also means a limb, a part of a body, and some readers say that fits a book treated as a living Guru. Now feel the opening the way a reader does. Hands washed, head covered. The rumala, the cloth over the book, folded back. The pages turned to the front. And the first thing the eyes meet isn't a sentence. At the top of ang one is a single sign, Ik Onkar, and it begins with the numeral one. Something to tell someone tonight: the Granth opens on a number before it opens on a word. Why start there, and not at a favorite hymn? A daily hukamnama opens wherever the book falls. A favorite hymn is easy to find. But a full reading that begins at ang one meets everything in the Guru's own order: the daily prayers first, then the ragas, the hard pages with the loved ones. Nothing gets skipped because it's unfamiliar. The weeks ahead walk that order, page by page. Begin at the beginning.
screen: `ANG: A PAGE, AND A LIMB.` · `HANDS, HEAD, CLOTH, FIRST PAGE.` · `BEFORE A WORD, THE NUMBER ONE.` · `THE GURU'S ORDER, NOTHING SKIPPED.` · then, large: `BEGIN AT THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: If you have a gutka or the Granth on a screen, open it to the very first page slowly, as if folding back a cloth, and let your eyes rest on the first sign before any words. If not, trace the shape of the number one in the air with a finger, slowly, top to bottom. Breathe while you trace it, and let one be all you hold.
Opening at ang 1. Starting a reading where the Guru starts: the first page, the first sign, the number one. Today's word.
Keep this: begin at the beginning, and let the Guru set the order of the pages. Rest well.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape senses. The opening of the book (washed hands, covered head, the rumala folded back, the first sign) carries the idea; the practice traces the numeral one or rests the eyes on ang 1.
Ang as 'limb' and 'some readers say that fits a book treated as a living Guru': hedged; confirm.
Surprising fact: ੴ begins with the numeral ੧, so the Granth opens on a number before a word. Confirm phrasing.
'The daily prayers first, then the ragas' describes the Granth's arrangement (Japji, So Dar/So Purakh, Sohila, then Sri Rag from Ang 14).
Ik Onkar is named but not explained; day 1447 (Ang 1: the Mool Mantar) opens it.
